book.title: Now, Discover Your Strengths
book.author: Marcus Buckingham and Donald O. Clifton

confidence_note: Two assumptions, the best managers' opposite pair, the interview groups and the 80,000-manager study are from Gallup's January 2001 excerpt and the book's introduction text. The 25-year/34-theme profile detail and the parents-and-teachers claim come from a summary page. Old claims (A in math/F in English report card, strengths give ten times the improvement, successful people manage weaknesses) were not found and dropped.
facts: Over thirty years Gallup interviewed 80,000 managers in hundreds of organizations to find what the best had in common; findings in First, Break All the Rules.

Gallup's study of excellence ran to a little over two million interviews: best teachers, doctors, salespeople, lawyers, professional basketball players, stockbrokers, accountants, hotel housekeepers, leaders, soldiers, nurses, pastors, systems engineers, chief executives.
Most organizations are built on two assumptions: each person can learn to be competent in almost anything; each person's greatest room for growth is in the areas of greatest weakness.
The best managers assume instead: each person's talents are enduring and unique; each person's greatest room for growth is in the areas of greatest strength.
The authors argue that parents, teachers, managers and psychology's focus on pathology make us experts in our weaknesses while strengths stay dormant and neglected.
A weakness is anything that gets in the way of excellent performance.
The StrengthsFinder profile came from about 25 years of Gallup work, identifies 34 themes and reports a person's five most powerful signature themes; the goal is consistent, near-perfect performance.

Gallup's four warning signs: more spent on training after hiring than on selection; performance managed through work rules, policies, procedures; development plans around areas of opportunity; promotion on accumulated skills with most prestige and pay to the most well-rounded. Remedial fixes such as a communication class are damage control, accepted only occasionally.
The best managers look for talent in every role, focus on outcomes, treat employees differently and spend the most time with the best people.
scene_details: hotel housekeepers and professional basketball players among the interview groups
two assumptions set against the opposite two
tension: Most organizations put growth effort where people are weakest; Gallup's best managers put it where people are strongest.
opening_idea: Two assumptions most organizations run on, and the opposite pair the best managers used.

lessons.idea: Look for growth where the person is strongest and manage the weak spot rather than fix it forever.
lessons.anchor: Best managers' assumption: greatest room for growth is in areas of greatest strength.

reflect_final: If you gave the work you do best a little more of next week's time, which task would you take off your calendar?

use_cases.situation: A meeting is called to fix a colleague's weak spot
use_cases.move: Cite Gallup's best managers, who put growth where a person is strongest, and ask what that person does best.

use_cases.situation: An employee struggles with one task again
use_cases.move: Arrange that task to weigh on them least and talk about what they do best.

use_cases.situation: You are writing your own development plan
use_cases.move: Ask whether the effort on your weak spots is matched by effort on your best work.

pocket_idea: Gallup's best managers looked for growth in strengths, not weaknesses.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Most organizations assume growth is in weakness; the best managers assume it is in strength.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Interview groups, two assumptions and the opposite pair, the five themes.
